title: Swap the to-do list
hook: A search keeps a list of places to visit. Change how you pull from it and see what shifts.

knows: BFS spreads in waves (wave-from-the-corner) and DFS goes deep (maze-depth-first)
a stack is last in, first out and a queue is first in, first out (back-button-stack)
doesNotKnow: that breadth-first and depth-first search are one algorithm with one line changed
that a queue finishes each ring before the next, which is why it finds fewest-hop routes

misconception: Breadth-first and depth-first search are two different algorithms that must be learned separately.
objective: The learner can explain that the same search with a queue or a stack as its to-do list visits the same six places in different orders, and that the queue's ring-by-ring order is why it finds routes with the fewest hops.

claims.text: On the graph A-B, A-C, B-D, B-E, C-F, E-F, starting from A and adding unseen neighbours in alphabetical order, the queue takes places in the order A B C D E F and the stack takes them in the order A C F E B D.
claims.source: Builder's node script (one loop, pop() for the stack, shift() for the queue, a place is marked when added to the to-do list): queue A B C D E F, stack A C F E B D. Corrects the brief, which said A C F B E D (that order needs one-way edges). Demo.tsx run() computes both. TheAlgorithms/Python used only as a reference for BFS/DFS behaviour, no code copied.

claims.text: Both runs reach all six places.
claims.source: Same node script: both orders contain A to F. CLRS 22.2 and 22.3: BFS and DFS visit every node reachable from the start.

claims.text: Look at the circled E: the queue found it 2 hops from A (through B), the stack 3 (through C and F).
claims.source: Builder's node script, hops recorded when a place is added to the to-do list: queue E=2 via B, stack E=3 via F; queue hops A0 B1 C1 D2 E2 F2, stack A0 B1 C1 F2 E3 D2. The true shortest A-to-E distance is 2. | r5 revision 2026-10-14: sentence reworded for v3; needs a fresh check. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 21): verified. Re-ran Demo.tsx run(): queue E hops 2 from B; stack E hops 3, from F, F from C (A-C-F-E). Reveal wording matches.

claims.text: A queue takes places ring by ring, which is why a search with a queue finds routes with the fewest hops.
claims.source: CLRS 3rd ed. section 22.2: BFS visits nodes in nondecreasing distance from the source; Theorem 22.5 (BFS computes shortest-path distances in unweighted graphs). The stack's route to E (3 hops) is longer than the true 2.

claims.text: Both runs use the same steps: take a place, add its unseen neighbours; the only difference is taking from the front (queue) or from the top (stack).
claims.source: Demo.tsx run(fromTop): one loop, the only branch is todo.pop() versus todo.shift(). Stack order here marks a place when added, which on this graph equals recursive DFS order (A C F E B D); the lesson says 'goes deep first', not 'is exactly depth-first search'.

recall.question: A search takes places from a to-do list and adds each place's unseen neighbours. Which change makes it visit the nearest places first, ring by ring?
options: Take from the front of the list (a queue)
Take from the top of the list (a stack)
recall.why: A queue serves places in the order they were added, so everything one hop away is taken before anything two hops away. A stack takes the newest place and goes deep first.
